coupled-reactions-s1.title: Getting copper from its ore
coupled-reactions-s1.html:
Copper can be obtained from the mineral chalcocite, Cu₂S. Data at 298 K:

Two reactions and their standard free energy changes at 298 K
ReactionEquationΔG° (kJ/mol)
1Cu₂S(s) → 2 Cu(s) + S(s)+86.2
2S(s) + O₂(g) → SO₂(g)−300.1

coupled-reactions-s2.title: Using ATP in a cell
coupled-reactions-s2.html:
Cells store energy in ATP. The first step of breaking down glucose attaches a phosphate group to glucose. Standard free energy changes at pH 7 (the standard state biochemists use), taken here for 37 °C (310 K):

Step A: glucose + phosphate → glucose-6-phosphate + H₂O; ΔG° = +13.8 kJ/mol
Step B: ATP + H₂O → ADP + phosphate; ΔG° = −30.5 kJ/mol
Overall: glucose + ATP → glucose-6-phosphate + ADP

Key: arrows show each step; the number on each is ΔG° in kJ/mol.

electrochemical-cells-s1.title: An iron-silver cell
electrochemical-cells-s1.html: A student builds the cell below. Beaker 1 holds an iron strip in 1.0 M Fe(NO₃)₂; Beaker 2 holds a silver strip in 1.0 M AgNO₃. The strips are joined by a wire through a voltmeter, and the beakers by a salt bridge of KNO₃(aq). The voltmeter shows a steady reading. After an hour the silver strip has gained mass and the iron strip has lost mass.

electrochemical-cells-s2.title: Metal strips in solutions
electrochemical-cells-s2.html:
A student places a clean metal strip in each of six solutions and records whether a coating forms on the strip after 10 minutes.

Observations for metal strips in 1.0 M solutions

2CuZn(NO₃)₂no change
3CuAgNO₃gray coating of Ag forms
4AgCu(NO₃)₂no change
5ZnAgNO₃gray coating of Ag forms
6AgZn(NO₃)₂no change

cell-potential-s2.title: An aluminum-copper cell
cell-potential-s2.html: A galvanic cell is built under standard conditions from an Al strip in 1.0 M Al(NO₃)₃ and a Cu strip in 1.0 M Cu(NO₃)₂. Standard reduction potentials: Al³⁺(aq) + 3e⁻ → Al(s), E° = −1.66 V; Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → Cu(s), E° = +0.34 V. F = 96,485 C/mol e⁻.

nernst-equation-s1.title: A zinc-copper cell at different concentrations
nernst-equation-s1.html:
A student measures the voltage of the cell Zn(s) | Zn²⁺(aq) || Cu²⁺(aq) | Cu(s), which runs Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s) with E° = 1.10 V, at 25 °C with different starting concentrations.

nernst-equation-s2.title: A concentration cell
nernst-equation-s2.html: Both beakers contain a copper strip in Cu(NO₃)₂(aq), but at different concentrations: 0.010 M in Beaker 1 and 1.0 M in Beaker 2. The voltmeter reads a small positive voltage.

electrolysis-faraday-s1.title: Copper plating a key
electrolysis-faraday-s1.html: A student plates copper onto a brass key. The key and a copper strip dip into 1.0 M CuSO₄(aq) and are connected to a power supply. A steady current of 2.50 A runs for 30.0 minutes. Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → Cu(s). Molar mass of Cu = 63.55 g/mol; F = 96,485 C/mol e⁻.

electrolysis-faraday-s2.title: Three cells in series
electrolysis-faraday-s2.html:
Three electrolytic cells are connected one after another (in series), so the same charge, 1.93 × 10⁴ C, passes through each. F = 96,485 C/mol e⁻.

items.q: Is Reaction 1 thermodynamically favored at 298 K on its own?
options: Yes: it makes three moles of product from one mole of reactant.
No: ΔG° > 0, so heating Cu₂S by itself does not give copper.
Yes: decompositions like this are favored at room temperature.
No: it is favored, but too slow to observe.

items.q: Calculate ΔG° for the overall reaction Cu₂S(s) + O₂(g) → 2 Cu(s) + SO₂(g).

mistakes.why: Sign: add the two ΔG° values with their own signs: +86.2 + (−300.1).
Value: Reaction 1 is used as written, so its ΔG° stays +86.2 kJ/mol.

items.q: Why does coupling Reaction 1 with Reaction 2 allow copper to be produced?
options: Reaction 2 releases heat that changes ΔG° of Reaction 1 to a negative value.
Reaction 2 acts as a catalyst for Reaction 1, lowering its activation energy.
Oxygen makes Cu₂S less stable, so Reaction 1 becomes favored without Reaction 2.
They share S(s): Reaction 2 uses the S that Reaction 1 makes; total ΔG° < 0.

items.q: K₁ for Reaction 1 is about 8 × 10⁻¹⁶ and K₂ for Reaction 2 is about 4 × 10⁵² at 298 K. What is K for the overall reaction?
options: About 3 × 10³⁷, the product K₁ × K₂
About 4 × 10⁵², the sum K₁ + K₂
About 5 × 10⁶⁷, the ratio K₂ ÷ K₁
About −213.9, the overall ΔG° value in kJ/mol

items.q: Calculate ΔG° for the overall coupled reaction, glucose + ATP → glucose-6-phosphate + ADP.

mistakes.why: Sign: Step B has ΔG° = −30.5 kJ/mol; add it with its sign.

items.q: Which statement best explains how the cell makes Step A happen?
options: It adds an enzyme that makes ΔG° for Step A negative.
It raises the temperature to 37 °C, which makes Step A favored on its own.
It couples Step A to ATP hydrolysis, so the overall ΔG° is negative.
It removes glucose-6-phosphate, so ΔG for Step A becomes zero.

items.q: Calculate K for the overall coupled reaction at 310 K. (R = 8.314 J/(mol·K))

mistakes.why: Value: that is K for Step A alone. Use the overall ΔG°, −16.7 kJ/mol.
Value: the data are for 310 K. Use T = 310 K, not 298 K.

items.q: If a cell paired Step A with a reaction that had ΔG° = −10.0 kJ/mol instead of ATP hydrolysis (with a suitable shared species), would the overall process be favored?
options: Yes: any favored reaction can drive any unfavored one.
Yes: the two ΔG° values multiply to a negative number.
No: +13.8 + (−10.0) = +3.8 kJ/mol, still positive.
No: coupled reactions need ΔG values of exactly equal size.

items.q: What must two reactions share to be coupled?
options: A species that one reaction makes and the other uses
The same activation energy
The same value of ΔG°
The same container, whatever the species involved

items.q: Water does not decompose into H₂ and O₂ on its own at 25 °C, but it does when a battery drives a current through it. What does the current do?
options: It changes ΔG° of the decomposition from positive to negative.
It lowers the activation energy, the way a catalyst does.
It heats the water until the decomposition becomes favored.
It supplies electrical energy that drives the reaction even though ΔG° > 0.

items.q: Plants make glucose from CO₂ and H₂O, a process with a large positive ΔG°. What makes this possible?
options: Plants lower the activation energy with enzymes, which makes ΔG° negative.
Absorbed light energy drives it through a chain of coupled steps.
The reaction becomes favored at the temperature of a leaf.
The glucose is removed as it forms, so ΔG° becomes zero.

items.q: Reaction 1: X → Y, ΔG° = +25.0 kJ/mol. Reaction 2: Y → Z, ΔG° = −40.0 kJ/mol. Calculate ΔG° for X → Z.

mistakes.why: Sign: the ΔG° values add with their signs: +25.0 + (−40.0).

items.q: A student says: "If we couple an unfavored reaction to a favored one, the unfavored reaction becomes favored." Which correction is best?
options: The unfavored step keeps its ΔG°; the overall process has ΔG° < 0.
The student is right: the favored reaction transfers its negative ΔG° to the other one.
Coupling makes both reactions unfavored, so neither occurs.
Coupling works by catalysis, so it changes rates, not ΔG°.

items.q: Reaction 1 has K₁ = 4.0 × 10⁻⁶ and Reaction 2 has K₂ = 2.5 × 10⁹. The two reactions add together to give Reaction 3. What is K₃, and is Reaction 3 product-favored?
options: K₃ = 2.5 × 10⁹; yes, because the larger K wins
K₃ = 6.3 × 10¹⁴; yes, because K₂ ÷ K₁ is large
K₃ = 1.0 × 10⁴; yes, because K₃ > 1
K₃ = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁵; no, because K₁ ÷ K₂ is small

items.q: Which can drive a process that has ΔG° > 0? Select ALL that apply.
options: Coupling it to a reaction with a more negative ΔG°
Supplying electrical energy from an outside source
Adding a catalyst
Waiting a long time

items.q: Which strip is the anode, and which process happens there?
options: The silver strip, where Ag⁺(aq) is reduced to Ag(s)
The iron strip, where Fe(s) is oxidized to Fe²⁺(aq)
The iron strip, where Fe²⁺(aq) is reduced to Fe(s)
The silver strip, where Ag(s) is oxidized to Ag⁺(aq)

items.q: Which is the balanced net ionic equation for the reaction in the cell?
options: Fe(s) + Ag⁺(aq) → Fe²⁺(aq) + Ag(s)
Fe²⁺(aq) + 2 Ag(s) → Fe(s) + 2 Ag⁺(aq)
Fe(s) + 2 AgNO₃(aq) → Fe(NO₃)₂(aq) + 2 Ag(s)
Fe(s) + 2 Ag⁺(aq) → Fe²⁺(aq) + 2 Ag(s)

items.q: In which direction do electrons flow through the wire?
options: From the iron strip to the silver strip
From the silver strip to the iron strip
Through the salt bridge from Beaker 1 to Beaker 2
They stay put; ions alone move in a cell

items.q: As the cell runs, which way do K⁺ and NO₃⁻ ions move out of the salt bridge?
options: K⁺ into Beaker 1 and NO₃⁻ into Beaker 2
Both ions into Beaker 2, where silver is plating out
K⁺ into Beaker 2 and NO₃⁻ into Beaker 1
Neither: the salt bridge lets electrons, not ions, cross between beakers

items.q: The salt bridge is lifted out while the wire stays connected. What happens to the voltmeter reading, and why?
options: It stays the same, because electrons can still flow through the wire.
It increases, because iron and silver ions can no longer mix.
It drops to zero: charge builds up in each beaker and the reaction stops.
It reverses sign, because the electrons flow back the other way.

items.q: In Trial 1, which species is oxidized?
options: Zn(s)
Cu²⁺(aq)
NO₃⁻(aq)
Cu(s)

items.q: A galvanic cell is built from a Cu strip in Cu(NO₃)₂(aq) and an Ag strip in AgNO₃(aq). Based on the trials, which electrode is the anode?
options: Silver, because Trial 4 shows silver does not react with Cu²⁺
Silver, because silver is the more valuable metal
Copper, because copper has the larger mass of the two metals
Copper, because in Trial 3 Cu(s) gives electrons to Ag⁺

items.q: Which ranks the metals from the one most easily oxidized to the one least easily oxidized?
options: Ag > Cu > Zn
Zn > Cu > Ag
Cu > Zn > Ag
Zn > Ag > Cu

items.q: If a strip of Ag is placed in Zn(NO₃)₂(aq), as in Trial 6, and connected to a power supply that forces zinc metal to plate onto it, what kind of cell is this?
options: An electrolytic cell: outside energy drives an unfavored reaction
A galvanic cell, because a metal plates onto an electrode
A galvanic cell, because the power supply produces a current
Neither, because a reaction that is not favored will not happen

items.q: In any electrochemical cell, galvanic or electrolytic, where does reduction take place?
options: At the anode
In the salt bridge
At the cathode
In the wire

items.q: Which statement correctly compares a galvanic cell with an electrolytic cell?
options: In a galvanic cell the anode is where reduction happens; in an electrolytic cell it is where oxidation happens.
Galvanic: a favored reaction makes a current. Electrolytic: outside energy drives an unfavored one.
A galvanic cell needs a power supply; an electrolytic cell produces its own current.
Electrons flow from the cathode to the anode in a galvanic cell and the other way in an electrolytic cell.

items.q: A galvanic cell is made from a Ni strip in Ni²⁺(aq) and a Sn strip in Sn²⁺(aq). As it runs, the nickel strip loses mass. What happens to [Sn²⁺] in the tin half-cell?
options: It increases, because tin is oxidized at the anode
It stays the same, because the salt bridge replaces each Sn²⁺ ion
It increases, because Ni²⁺ ions cross the salt bridge and become Sn²⁺
It decreases, because Sn²⁺ ions are reduced to Sn(s) at the cathode

items.q: Which are needed for a galvanic cell to produce a steady current? Select ALL that apply.
options: A favored redox reaction split into two half-reactions in separate compartments
An external wire connecting the two electrodes
A salt bridge or porous barrier that lets ions move
A power supply that pushes electrons into the anode
The same metal ion in both compartments
A reaction with ΔG° > 0

items.q: If the iron strip and the AgNO₃ solution of a cell were simply put in the same beaker, silver would plate onto the iron, but no useful current would flow. Why?
options: The reaction is no longer favored when the reactants are in the same beaker.
Silver ions are unable to reach the iron strip without a salt bridge.
Iron is reduced instead of oxidized when it touches AgNO₃ directly.
Electrons pass straight from Fe atoms to Ag⁺ ions, not through a wire.

items.q: In an electrolytic cell used to coat a steel spoon with silver, which electrode is the spoon, and why?
options: The anode, because the spoon is oxidized so that it holds the silver
The cathode, because Ag⁺ ions must be reduced onto the spoon
The cathode, because electrons leave the spoon through the wire
The anode, because silver is plated wherever oxidation happens

items.q: A galvanic cell runs the reaction Zn(s) + Pb²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Pb(s). Which half-reaction occurs at the cathode?
options: Zn(s) → Zn²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻
Pb(s) → Pb²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻
Pb²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → Pb(s)
Zn²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → Zn(s)

items.q: A galvanic cell is built from a Ni/Ni²⁺ half-cell and an Ag/Ag⁺ half-cell under standard conditions. Calculate E°cell.

mistakes.why: Value: you doubled E° for silver because its half-reaction is doubled. E° is intensive: balancing electrons never changes it.
Value: you added the two reduction potentials. Use E°cell = E°(cathode) − E°(anode).
Sign: in a galvanic cell the cathode is the half-reaction with the more positive E°, so E°cell is positive.

items.q: Which is the balanced overall reaction for the Ni/Ag galvanic cell?
options: Ni²⁺(aq) + 2 Ag(s) → Ni(s) + 2 Ag⁺(aq)
Ni(s) + 2 Ag⁺(aq) → Ni²⁺(aq) + 2 Ag(s)
Ni(s) + Ag⁺(aq) → Ni²⁺(aq) + Ag(s)
Ni(s) + 2 Ag(s) → Ni²⁺(aq) + 2 Ag⁺(aq)

items.q: Calculate ΔG° for the reaction in the Ni/Ag cell, Ni(s) + 2 Ag⁺(aq) → Ni²⁺(aq) + 2 Ag(s).

mistakes.why: Value: n is the moles of electrons transferred in the balanced equation: 2, not 1.
Sign: ΔG° = −nFE°. A positive E°cell gives a negative ΔG°.

items.q: Which pair of half-cells from the table would give the largest E°cell?
options: Al/Al³⁺ and Cu/Cu²⁺
Zn/Zn²⁺ and Ag/Ag⁺
Pb/Pb²⁺ and Mg/Mg²⁺
Mg/Mg²⁺ and Ag/Ag⁺

items.q: Which species in the table is the strongest reducing agent?
options: Mg(s)
Ag⁺(aq)
Mg²⁺(aq)
Ag(s)

items.q: Calculate E°cell for the cell.

mistakes.why: Value: you multiplied each E° by its coefficient (3 Cu²⁺, 2 Al). E° is intensive and is never multiplied.
Value: you added the reduction potentials. Subtract the anode’s E° from the cathode’s.

items.q: How many moles of electrons, n, are transferred in the balanced equation 2 Al(s) + 3 Cu²⁺(aq) → 2 Al³⁺(aq) + 3 Cu(s)?
Calculate ΔG° for 2 Al(s) + 3 Cu²⁺(aq) → 2 Al³⁺(aq) + 3 Cu(s).

mistakes.why: Value: n = 6 mol e⁻ for this equation (2 Al × 3e⁻), not 2.
Value: n = 6 mol e⁻ for this equation (3 Cu²⁺ × 2e⁻), not 3.
Value: you used an E° multiplied by coefficients (4.34 V). Use E°cell = 2.00 V; the coefficients enter only through n.

items.q: A student writes E°cell = 3(+0.34) − 2(−1.66) = 4.34 V "because the equation has 3 Cu²⁺ and 2 Al." Which correction is best?
options: The coefficients should be divided, not multiplied, giving 0.34/3 + 1.66/2.
The student is right; the coefficients belong in E° and in n as well.
E° is intensive, like temperature, so coefficients never change it: E°cell = 2.00 V.
The anode’s E° alone should be multiplied, because electrons are released there.

items.q: For a redox reaction at standard conditions, which set of signs goes together?
options: E°cell > 0, ΔG° < 0, K > 1
E°cell > 0, ΔG° > 0, K < 1
E°cell < 0, ΔG° < 0, K > 1
E°cell > 0, ΔG° < 0, K < 1

items.q: For Cu(s) + Zn²⁺(aq) → Cu²⁺(aq) + Zn(s), E° = −1.10 V. What does this tell you?
options: The reaction is favored but slow, so it needs a catalyst.
The cell will run with electrons flowing from Zn to Cu, so it is still galvanic.
The reaction is at equilibrium, because E° is negative.
It is not favored; it needs an electrolytic cell with a power supply.

items.q: For Cu(s) + 2 Ag⁺(aq) → Cu²⁺(aq) + 2 Ag(s), E° = +0.46 V at 298 K. Calculate K. (F = 96,485 C/mol e⁻; R = 8.314 J/(mol·K))

mistakes.why: Value: n = 2 mol e⁻ for this equation (one Cu gives two electrons).

items.q: A galvanic cell made from a metal M in 1.0 M M²⁺ and Cu in 1.0 M Cu²⁺ has E°cell = 0.74 V. M is the anode. E° for Cu²⁺/Cu is +0.34 V. Calculate the standard reduction potential of M²⁺/M.

mistakes.why: Value: E°cell = E°(cathode) − E°(anode), so E°(anode) = 0.34 − 0.74, not 0.34 + 0.74.
Sign: M is the anode, so its reduction potential is lower than copper’s.

items.q: Reaction 1 is Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s), with E° = 1.10 V and ΔG° = −212 kJ/mol. Reaction 2 is the same reaction with every coefficient doubled. What are E° and ΔG° for Reaction 2?

Use these standard reduction potentials: Ag⁺/Ag +0.80 V, Cu²⁺/Cu +0.34 V, Ni²⁺/Ni −0.25 V, Zn²⁺/Zn −0.76 V. Which reactions are thermodynamically favored under standard conditions? Select ALL that apply.
options: Zn(s) + Ni²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Ni(s)
Cu(s) + Ni²⁺(aq) → Cu²⁺(aq) + Ni(s)
Cu(s) + Zn²⁺(aq) → Cu²⁺(aq) + Zn(s)
2 Ag(s) + Zn²⁺(aq) → 2 Ag⁺(aq) + Zn(s)

items.q: In ΔG° = −nFE°, what does n stand for?
options: The moles of electrons transferred in the balanced overall equation
The number of moles of metal that plate out at the cathode
The number of half-reactions in the cell, which is 2
The charge on the cation formed at the anode

items.q: In which trial is the cell at standard conditions, so that E = E°?
options: Trial 3, where the voltage is highest
Trial 1, where both ions are 1.0 M and Q = 1
Trial 5, where the voltage is lowest
Each of the five trials, because each is at 25 °C

items.q: Which statement explains why E is greater than E° in Trials 2 and 3?
options: Less Zn²⁺ means fewer ions in solution, so the electrons meet less resistance in the wire.
E° itself increases when [Zn²⁺] decreases.
The reaction reaches equilibrium faster when [Zn²⁺] is low.
Q < 1, so the cell is further from equilibrium and its drive is greater.

items.q: A sixth trial uses [Zn²⁺] = 0.50 M and [Cu²⁺] = 0.050 M. How does its voltage compare with E°?
options: Less than 1.10 V, because Q = 10 > 1
Greater than 1.10 V, because both concentrations are below 1 M
Equal to 1.10 V, because neither concentration is zero
Zero, because the concentrations are not equal

items.q: The cell from Trial 1 is left running until it no longer lights a bulb. What are E and Q at that point?
options: E = E° and Q = 1, because the reaction has stopped
E = 0 and Q = 0, because one reactant is used up
E = 0 and Q = K: the reaction is at equilibrium
E is negative and Q > K, because the reaction runs backward

items.q: What is E°cell for this concentration cell?
options: 0.34 V, the E° of the copper half-reaction
0.68 V, the copper E° added for both electrodes
0 V, since both electrodes share one half-reaction
It has to be looked up in a reduction potential table

items.q: In which beaker is copper metal oxidized?
options: Beaker 1, the dilute side, where [Cu²⁺] then rises
Beaker 2, the concentrated solution, so Cu²⁺ is produced there
Both beakers equally, so the voltage is zero
Neither, because a cell with one metal has no anode

items.q: What happens to the voltage of the concentration cell as it runs for a long time?
options: It rises, because more Cu²⁺ ions are made.
It stays constant, because E°cell is constant.
It becomes negative once Beaker 1 has more Cu²⁺ than Beaker 2.
It falls toward zero as the two concentrations become equal.

items.q: If Beaker 1 were made even more dilute, 0.0010 M, how would the initial voltage change?
options: It would decrease, because there are fewer ions to carry charge
It would increase, because Q = 0.0010 is further below 1
It would stay the same, because E°cell is still zero
It would become zero, because the solution is too dilute to react

items.q: For a galvanic cell, how does E compare with E° when Q > 1?
options: E is smaller than E°
E is larger than E°
E equals E°
E is zero

items.q: A galvanic cell runs Ni(s) + 2 Ag⁺(aq) → Ni²⁺(aq) + 2 Ag(s), starting at standard conditions. Predict the effect of each change on the measured cell potential, E.

variables.name: Adding solid AgNO₃ to the silver half-cell, raising [Ag⁺]
Adding solid Ni(NO₃)₂ to the nickel half-cell, raising [Ni²⁺]
Using a larger nickel strip of the same metal
Letting the cell run for an hour
Replacing the KNO₃ salt bridge with a NaNO₃ salt bridge

items.q: A student says a battery goes "dead" because it runs out of electrons. Which explanation is accurate?
options: The salt bridge runs out of ions, so the current stops while E stays the same.
E° slowly falls to zero as the metal electrodes wear down.
The reaction reaches equilibrium: Q = K, so E = 0.
The student is right: each electrode holds a fixed number of electrons.

items.q: The Nernst equation is E = E° − (RT/nF) ln Q. For a cell with E° > 0, which situation gives E = E°?
options: Q = 0, so the second term is zero
Q = 1, which makes ln Q = 0
Q = K, so the reaction is at equilibrium
T = 0 K, so RT/nF is zero

items.q: For Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s), which change raises the cell potential the most?
options: Lowering [Cu²⁺] to 0.010 M while keeping [Zn²⁺] at 1.0 M
Lowering both concentrations to 0.010 M
Using a zinc strip twice as large
Lowering [Zn²⁺] to 0.010 M, with [Cu²⁺] at 1.0 M

items.q: For a galvanic cell with E° > 0, which statements are true? Select ALL that apply.
options: When Q < 1, E > E°.
When the reaction reaches equilibrium, E = E°.
E° changes as concentrations change.
When Q > 1, E is negative.

items.q: Two Zn/Cu cells are built. Cell X has [Zn²⁺] = 0.10 M and [Cu²⁺] = 1.0 M. Cell Y has [Zn²⁺] = 1.0 M and [Cu²⁺] = 0.10 M. Which statement compares them correctly?
options: Cell Y has the larger voltage, because it has more Zn²⁺ to carry charge.
They have equal voltages, because each has one ion at 0.10 M.
They have equal voltages, because E° is the same for both.
Cell X has the larger voltage, because its Q is smaller.

items.q: How much charge, in coulombs, passes through the circuit?

mistakes.why: Value: you used 30.0 minutes as if it were seconds. Convert to 1800 s first: q = It needs t in seconds.

items.q: Calculate the mass of copper plated onto the key.

mistakes.why: Value: you left out the 2 mol e⁻ per mol Cu. Each Cu²⁺ needs two electrons, so divide moles of electrons by 2.
Value: time must be in seconds (1800 s), not minutes.
Value: you multiplied by 2. There are 2 mol e⁻ per mol Cu, so divide moles of electrons by 2.

items.q: Which electrode is the key, and what happens there?
options: The anode, where Cu²⁺ ions gain electrons and copper plates on
The cathode, where Cu²⁺ gains electrons and copper plates on
The cathode, where copper atoms lose electrons and dissolve
The anode, where copper atoms lose electrons and dissolve

items.q: How many minutes would it take to plate 2.00 g of copper at the same current?

mistakes.why: Units: that is the time in seconds. Divide by 60 to report minutes.
Value: you used 1 mol e⁻ per mol Cu. Copper(II) needs 2.

items.q: How many moles of electrons pass through each cell?

mistakes.why: Value: divide the charge by F (coulombs per mole of electrons); do not multiply.

items.q: What mass of aluminum is produced in Cell 3?

mistakes.why: Value: Al³⁺ needs 3 mol e⁻ per mol Al. Divide the moles of electrons by 3.
Value: you multiplied by 3. Three electrons are needed for each Al, so divide.

items.q: Which cell produces the greatest mass of metal, and why?
options: Cell 3: aluminum ions carry the largest charge, so they attract the most electrons.
The three masses are equal, because the same charge passes through each cell.
Cell 2: copper is between silver and aluminum, so it balances charge and mass best.
Cell 1: Ag⁺ needs one electron, giving the most moles, and Ag is heaviest.

items.q: What is the ratio of moles of Ag : Cu : Al produced?
What does the Faraday constant, F = 96,485 C/mol e⁻, represent?
options: The charge carried by one electron
The current that plates one mole of metal per second
The charge carried by one mole of electrons
The voltage needed to plate one mole of metal

items.q: A car part is chrome-plated from a Cr³⁺ solution (Cr³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Cr). If 1.80 × 10⁴ C pass through the cell, what mass of chromium (52.00 g/mol) is deposited? (F = 96,485 C/mol e⁻)

mistakes.why: Value: each Cr³⁺ needs 3 electrons. Divide mol e⁻ by 3 before converting to grams.

items.q: What constant current deposits 0.500 g of silver (107.87 g/mol) from Ag⁺(aq) in 600. s? (F = 96,485 C/mol e⁻)

mistakes.why: Value: that is the charge. Divide by the time, 600. s, to get the current.

items.q: An aluminum smelting cell runs at 1.00 × 10⁵ A for 1.00 hour. Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al (26.98 g/mol). What mass of aluminum, in kilograms, does it produce? (F = 96,485 C/mol e⁻)

mistakes.why: Units: that is grams. Divide by 1000 for kilograms.
Value: each Al³⁺ needs three electrons. Divide moles of electrons by 3.
Value: 1.00 hour is 3600 s, not 60 s.

items.q: Two students electrolyze molten NaCl (2 Na⁺ + 2 Cl⁻ → 2 Na + Cl₂) with the same current for the same time. Which statement about the products is correct?
options: Equal moles of Na and Cl₂ form, because the same current passes both electrodes.
Twice as many moles of Cl₂ as of Na form, because chlorine is a diatomic gas.
Twice as many moles of Na as Cl₂: 1 e⁻ per Na, but 2 e⁻ per Cl₂.
No sodium forms, because the reaction is not thermodynamically favored.

items.q: A student plates copper and finds the key gained less mass than calculated from the current and time. Which is a plausible cause?
options: Some current went into another reduction at the cathode, such as making H₂.
The student used a larger key, which needs more copper.
The copper anode lost mass during the run.
The CuSO₄ solution was more concentrated than 1.0 M.

items.q: Doubling which quantity, with everything else unchanged, halves the mass of metal plated?
options: The current through the cell
The time the current runs
The molar mass of the metal plated
The number of electrons needed by each metal ion

items.q: In the plating of copper from Cu²⁺, which sequence of conversions takes you from current and time to mass?
options: I × t → coulombs → × F → mol e⁻ → × 2 → mol Cu → × 63.55 → g Cu
I × t → coulombs → ÷ F → mol e⁻ → ÷ 2 → mol Cu → × 63.55 → g Cu
I ÷ t → coulombs → ÷ F → mol e⁻ → ÷ 2 → mol Cu → × 63.55 → g Cu
I × t → coulombs → ÷ F → mol Cu → × 63.55 → g Cu
